title: Find Your Dream Job: Insider Tips for Finding Work, Advancing your Career, and Loving Your Job
author: Mac Prichard
description: Build a career that matters to you with job search strategies and career advice from Find Your Dream Job. Host Mac Prichard of Mac's List interviews career experts weekly on landing great jobs and building purposeful careers.

episodes.title: Resume Hacks That Impress HR Directors with Derek Murphy-Johnson
episodes.summary: HR director Derek Murphy-Johnson explains why generic resumes fail and how to customise each one using the job description's keywords and language, while keeping formatting simple and typo-free.

episodes.title: How To Move into a New Role (In or Outside Your Field), with Amelia Badua
episodes.summary: Career specialist Amelia Badua walks through identifying target roles, building materials that address employer needs, and using AI prompts to surface transferable skills and tailor a resume.

episodes.title: Stop Waiting to Be Picked: The 3 Questions That Can Transform Your Job Search, with Jamila Brown
episodes.summary: Jamila Brown's three questions for a focused search: what you want, where you're going, and what you offer. She explains why networking and informational interviews beat cold applications.

episodes.title: Words to Use and Lose in Your Next Job Interview, with Tracy Hooper
episodes.summary: Communication coach Tracy Hooper names the hedge words, fillers, disclaimers, and validators that undermine confidence in interviews, what to say instead, and a one-word-a-month method for changing habits.

episodes.title: How Executive Dysfunction Affects Your Job Search (And What to Do About It), with Ben Tobin
episodes.summary: Ben Tobin explains how executive dysfunction shows up as delayed applications, over-preparation, and endless planning, and how scheduling and smaller steps help job seekers get unstuck.

episodes.title: Should I Go Back to School to Get My Dream Job? with Ken Coleman
episodes.summary: Ken Coleman argues more education often isn't necessary for a dream role, and that networking, mentorship, and alternative learning paths can get you there without heavy student debt.

articles.question: What words should you avoid in a job interview?
articles.metaDescription: Communication coach Tracy Hooper, on Find Your Dream Job, lists the hedges, fillers, disclaimers, and validators that make candidates sound unsure, and what to say instead.
articles.intro: Drop the hedges, the fillers, the disclaimers, and the little requests for validation. That's the short list from communication coach Tracy Hooper on Find Your Dream Job with host Mac Prichard. Words like "just," "kind of," "I could be wrong, but," and "does that make sense?" quietly signal that you don't trust your own answer. Tracy explains why interviewers read those words as a lack of confidence, gives specific replacements, and offers a realistic plan for breaking the habit one word at a time.

sections.heading: Confidence is the thing every interviewer is listening for
sections.body:
Tracy's starting point is that hiring managers are scanning for confidence, whether they say so or not. They're asking themselves if this person will hold their own in a client meeting or a tough conversation with a colleague. Word choice is one of the fastest ways they form that impression.

She calls the good ones "becoming" words: language that fits a capable professional. The problem words fall into a few families, and most of us use them without noticing. Tracy admits she only discovered her own verbal tic after hearing a recording of herself, which is also her first piece of advice: record a practice answer and listen back.

quote.text: When we use these words, they don't make us sound as if we're confident, and that's what everyone is looking for.
quote.speaker: Tracy Hooper

sections.heading: Hedges and fillers: the words that shrink your answer
sections.body:
Fillers are the obvious ones: "um," "like," "you know," "really," and "so" at the start of every sentence. They're noise, and in an interview the noise gets counted.

Hedges are sneakier because they feel polite. "Just," "kind of," "a little bit," "sort of," "maybe," "I guess," "actually," and the catch-all "stuff." Tracy's point is that we reach for them to sound modest, but the listener doesn't hear modesty. They hear someone who isn't sure. "I just managed a small team" and "I managed a team of six" describe the same job, and only one of them sounds like a leader. She also flags "thing" as a word to retire, because it's vague where an interviewer wants specifics.

quote.text: Hedges are those words where we want to sound humble or modest but they don't make us sound confident.
quote.speaker: Tracy Hooper

sections.heading: Disclaimers, validators, and apologies
sections.body:
Disclaimers are the pre-emptive apologies for having an opinion: "correct me if I'm wrong," "you've been doing this longer than me," "what do I know," "just my two cents," "this might sound crazy." Each one hands the interviewer a reason to discount what comes next.

Validators are the tags at the end: "does that make sense?", "am I being clear?", "is that okay?", "do you see what I'm saying?" They ask the interviewer to reassure you. Tracy's replacements keep the invitation but drop the neediness: "Do you have questions?", "What are your thoughts?", "How is this landing with you?"

And then there's "I'm sorry," which many candidates use for things that need no apology, like taking a moment to think. Her swap is gratitude: "Thank you for your patience," "Thank you for understanding." One more she likes for a half-formed idea: "This thought is 30 seconds old," which signals candour without self-sabotage.

quote.text: When we use the same words as everybody else, then we sound like every other candidate.
quote.speaker: Tracy Hooper

sections.heading: What to say instead
sections.body:
For disclaimers, Tracy suggests ownership language: "In my experience," "Here's my perspective," "Let me know if I heard that correctly," "What if we try this," "Let's consider." These frame you as a peer contributing a view rather than a junior asking permission.

For talking about yourself, she recommends direct, declarative constructions: "I'm a quick learner," "My strength is," "People see me as," "I'm known for." These feel bold to say the first few times, which is exactly why they work. Interviewers hear a candidate who knows what they bring. Her reminder is that the company is interested in you specifically, so speak as the unique person they invited in.

quote.text: Companies want you. You're your unique person.
quote.speaker: Tracy Hooper

sections.heading: A month per word
sections.body:
Tracy is realistic about habit change. You won't purge a decade of "just" in a week, and trying to fix everything at once makes you self-conscious and stilted. Her method is one word or phrase per month. Pick the worst offender from your recording, notice it, replace it, and move on to the next one when it's gone.

She describes the payoff as a virtuous cycle. Cleaner language makes you sound more confident, people respond to you differently, and that response makes you feel more confident, which cleans up your language further. Paired with posture and presence, she says, it changes how much you're seen and heard, in interviews and after you get the job.

quote.text: Be kind to yourself, give yourself a month per word or phrase.
quote.speaker: Tracy Hooper

keyTakeaways: Cut fillers (um, like, you know, so) and hedges (just, kind of, sort of, maybe, I guess, stuff).
Drop disclaimers like "correct me if I'm wrong" and validators like "does that make sense?"
Replace apologies with thanks: "Thank you for your patience" instead of "I'm sorry."
Use ownership language: "In my experience," "My strength is," "I'm known for."
Record yourself, then fix one word or phrase per month rather than everything at once.

faq.q: Is it bad to say 'um' in a job interview?
faq.a: A few won't sink you, but Tracy Hooper lists fillers like "um," "like," and "you know" among the words that erode the impression of confidence. Record yourself to find out how often you use them.

faq.q: How do I stop saying 'just' all the time?
faq.a: Notice it first, ideally from a recording, then commit to replacing it for a month before moving on to the next habit. Tracy recommends one word or phrase per month.

faq.q: What should I say instead of 'does that make sense?'
faq.a: Tracy suggests "Do you have questions?", "What are your thoughts?", or "How is this landing with you?" These invite feedback without asking for reassurance.

articles.sourceNote: Based on "Words to Use and Lose in Your Next Job Interview" with Tracy Hooper, released September 2, 2026 on Find Your Dream Job (originally Episode 290, April 2021), hosted by Mac Prichard of Mac's List.
